problem_statement:
Fix registry cleanup thread shutdown

CleanupJob stored its Event in Thread._stop, so stopping and joining the thread raised TypeError during host shutdown. Rename the event to preserve the Thread method. The regression test fails before the fix and passes after it, including repeated stop/join.

- **Proposed target version:** next patch
- **Estimated release window:** next stable
- **Forward-port tracking issue (stable patches only):** N/A — mainline work

AI-assisted implementation using Codex. Verified the real thread lifecycle locally; broader integration is covered by CI. No new runtime dependencies or public API changes.

new file mode 100644
index 000000000..6bc9ef694
--- /dev/null
+++ b/docs/blog/2026-09-18-a-thread-that-cannot-join.md
@@ -0,0 +1,9 @@
+# A thread that could stop, but could not join
+
+The service restarted successfully, yet its shutdown log contained a TypeError. The cleanup thread had finished its loop. The failure came afterward, when Python tried to join it.
+
+The thread kept its cancellation event in `self._stop`. That name already belongs to `threading.Thread`: joining a finished thread calls its internal `_stop()` method. Our Event replaced that method, so normal shutdown tried to call an Event.
+
+Renaming the field to `_stop_event` leaves the standard thread lifecycle intact. A regression test starts a real cleanup thread, stops it twice, joins it again, and checks that it is no longer alive. Before the rename, the first stop fails with the same TypeError as the service. Afterward, all three waits succeed.
+
+A successful restart only proves the new process came up. It says nothing about whether the old process shut down cleanly. That distinction is why this test exercises the actual thread rather than mocking `join`.

problem_statement:
[1.8.5] The inbox record does not say which consumer handled a message

## Outcome

The inbox's own record says **which consumer** handled each message. Today it does not.

[code omitted]

Verified against `inbox/store.py` on main: `done()` writes `{"id", "at"}` and `record_sent()` writes seven fields, none of which identify the consumer.

## Why it matters now rather than later

Several consumers of one directory is not an edge case, it is the design. DD-063's whole argument is that the tool writes files and consumers arrive by themselves, and three ship today: `co ai --listen`, the Host lifespan, and `co <provider> consume -- <command>` with Claude Code, Codex or a script behind it. Taking a message is `rename(2)`, so they cannot collide — that part works and is tested.

What they can do is leave an indistinguishable trail. During development the normal setup is a Host answering in one terminal while a person drives `co feishu receive` in another to inspect something. When a group gets an answer nobody expected, or does not get one, the question is *which of them had it* — and the files cannot say.

The same gap makes a real failure unreadable. A message that came back after its lease expired, was picked up by a different consumer and answered twice looks in `sent.jsonl` like two replies with no explanation of why. With the consumer recorded it reads as what it is.

## Shape

One field on the durable records, and one line in the output.

- `done.jsonl` and `sent.jsonl` gain `by`: a short string naming the consumer — `host`, `co-ai`, `receive`, or `consume:<command basename>`.
- `Inbox.serve(handler, by=…)` takes it, so a consumer names itself once rather than at every call site. `receive` and `reply` invoked straight from a shell name themselves from the verb.
- `co <provider> ls` and `co <provider> log` show it where they already show a message's state.
- It is descriptive, not authorization: nothing decides anything on the strength of it, and a consumer that lies only mislabels its own work. Who may command an agent is #1479.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `done.jsonl` and `sent.jsonl` carry `by` for every writer in the tree — the Host lifespan, `co ai --listen`, `consume`, and a bare `receive`/`reply`/`done` from a shell
- [ ] A record written by an older version with no `by` still reads (absent, not crashing)
- [ ] Two consumers on one inbox, one message each: the records distinguish them, and a test asserts it
- [ ] A message handed out twice after a lease expiry shows both consumers
- [ ] `co feishu log` shows who handled the last few
- [ ] Nothing branches on the value

## Not in scope

Anything that treats `by` as identity or permission. It is a label on work that happened, the way a commit's author is.

problem_statement:
Fix RoboCasa EGL resource ownership during deferred cleanup

## Summary

Fix camera cross-talk / corrupted readback in Zetta's RoboCasa integration after deferred EGL context destruction. This PR contains only the renderer integration and its regression tests, not the experimental tiny-policy bridge or any checkpoint / rollout artifacts.

## Root cause

The deployed RoboSuite `MjRenderContext.__del__` frees its MuJoCo GL resources without first binding the owning EGL context. An old simulator can remain alive through cyclic references after reset. If its collection happens while the new simulator's context is current (observed during late tiny-policy loading), resource deletion can affect the new context's objects. Copying image arrays or removing forced observations cannot repair already-corrupted GL resources.

The failing control used zero forced observation refreshes and still produced camera swaps. Logging showed that the destroyed context and current context differed. Binding the owner before deletion and restoring the live context eliminated the failure in the matched fixed probe.

## Changes

- Install an idempotent, process-local EGL destructor fix before creating the environment's renderer; do not edit the shared RoboSuite installation.
- Save the current context/display/surfaces, bind the owner for MuJoCo and EGL cleanup, then restore a different live context.
- Avoid taking the renderer lock in the destructor: cyclic GC may execute on the thread already holding it.
- Serialize RGB render/readback through RoboSuite's existing offscreen context and return owned C-contiguous arrays, without creating another `mujoco.Renderer`.
- Preserve the public installer/cleanup entry points and delegate depth/segmentation/non-offscreen requests to the existing implementation.
- Test cleanup ownership, restoring another context, no prior/current-owner context, idempotence, partial initialization, and RGB frame ownership.

## Validation

Clean PR worktree based on upstream `main` (`0435ba6`):

[code omitted]

On RTX 4090, MuJoCo 3.3.1, target WashLettuce seed 126:

| Integration probe | Steps | Tiny steps | Same-step near-duplicate / cross-camera exact matches | Forced refreshes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Unfixed destructor control | 70 | 63 | 10 / 7 | 0 |
| Fixed destructor control | 70 | 63 | 0 / 0 | 0 |
| Fixed full session, zero actions after tiny | 1650 | 63 | 0 / 0 | 0 |
| Fixed session, recorded VLA actions in 16-action chunks | 200 | 63 | 0 / 0 | 0 |

Tiny reached `water_on=true` in every probe, without an episode reset at handoff. Cameras stayed enabled. The 1650-step test used EGL physical GPU 3 with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3,7`; the short replay used GPU 7.

The full test produced 1651 frames per camera and exactly 1650 per-camera step renders, with no detected black frames or discontinuities. All three MP4s passed the existing video artifact audit and full FFmpeg decoding. The 200-step moving-action replay also passed; handoff views were visually checked.

These integration runs used the isolated experimental tiny bridge with cached step observations and RGB-only cameras. They do **not** claim online GR00T inference, task success rates, depth/segmentation coverage, or a canonical evaluation. That bridge is intentionally excluded from this framework PR. No historical rollout attempt was changed.

RolloutWorker spawns fragmented small inference batches that queue on GPU under async eval

In async offline eval, RuntimeRolloutWorker repeatedly spawns small inference batches (often $$BS\approx2–3$$) while earlier batches are still running on the same GPU. These batches cannot be merged after spawn, so the GPU ends up executing a long queue of tiny forwards instead of fewer, larger ones.

Observed effects at high concurrency (level=16-48):
* Average batch size stays ~1.2–1.3 despite max_batch_size up to 14–16
* ~2000 inference batches for ~2560 policy steps, i.e., too small size per batch
* Overall throughput plateaus around ~15 steps/s even as session count increases

problem_statement:
[Bug] Torrra crashes with libtorrent ABI 2 due to ABI 1-only status APIs

### What happened?

Torrra crashes when used with Homebrew's libtorrent 2.1.1 bindings. There are three unconditional references to APIs that libtorrent only exposes in ABI 1 builds:

[code omitted]

The first two cause Torrra to crash while importing `DownloadManager`. After guarding those locally, Torrra starts but crashes again while processing torrent status because `torrent_status.error` is also unavailable.

Current v2.1.1 source still contains all three references.

### Version

- Torrra: current v2.1.1 source is affected
- Installed build where originally reproduced: `torrra, version 2.1.0` from Homebrew HEAD at `334edde`
- libtorrent Python bindings: `2.1.1.0`
- Homebrew formula: `libtorrent-rasterbar 2.1.1_1`
- Python: 3.14

### OS and architecture

macOS arm64

### Terminal Output or Logs

The initial startup failure is:

[code omitted]

After removing or guarding the two unavailable enum members, Torrra starts but later fails while processing torrent status:

[code omitted]

### Root cause

Libtorrent's Python bindings only export `queued_for_checking`, `allocating`, and `torrent_status.error` when compiled with:

[code omitted]

Homebrew's `libtorrent-rasterbar` is compiled with `TORRENT_ABI_VERSION=2`, so these members are absent. The supported ABI-2 status states are:

- `checking_files`
- `downloading_metadata`
- `downloading`
- `finished`
- `seeding`
- `checking_resume_data`

The locked PyPI `libtorrent==2.1.1` wheel used by the current CI workflow still exposes the ABI-1 compatibility members. This allows the test suite to pass without exercising the API surface provided by Homebrew and other system packages.

All three incompatible accesses were introduced together in PR 309.

This is the same compatibility pattern previously reported in [issue 285](https://github.com/stabldev/torrra/issues/285), where `torrent_handle.has_metadata()` was missing from a libtorrent 2.1 system build. [PR 288](https://github.com/stabldev/torrra/pull/288) fixed that specific call by switching to the non-deprecated status API, but it did not add coverage for bindings that omit ABI-1 members.

Libtorrent's binding definitions are available in [`bindings/python/src/torrent_status.cpp`](https://github.com/arvidn/libtorrent/blob/v2.1.1/bindings/python/src/torrent_status.cpp).

### Proposed fix

1. Build `_STATE_MAP` without unconditionally accessing `queued_for_checking` or `allocating`. These mappings can be added conditionally with `getattr` when an ABI-1 binding provides them.
2. Use `torrent_status.errc` as the primary error source. If compatibility with ABI-1 bindings still requires the legacy string, access it through `getattr(s, "error", None)`.
3. Update `tests/test_core_download.py` so it does not require the deprecated enum members to exist.
4. Add regression coverage using a state surface that omits all ABI-1-only members, or add an integration job against a system-provided ABI-2 libtorrent binding.
5. Publish the fix in a patch release so package managers can remove downstream workarounds.

### Expected behavior

Torrra should start and process torrent status normally with both PyPI's libtorrent wheel and ABI-2 system builds such as Homebrew's `libtorrent-rasterbar`.

### Acceptance criteria

- Importing `torrra.core.download` succeeds when `queued_for_checking` and `allocating` are absent.
- Searching and updating the downloads view succeeds when `torrent_status.error` is absent.
- Error reporting continues to use `torrent_status.errc`.
- Existing behavior remains compatible with the PyPI libtorrent wheel.
- Automated coverage prevents future unconditional use of ABI-1-only bindings.

problem_statement:
benchmarks: add elf_shoff prior probe (guessed ELF64 section-table offset) + fix --probe filter

Part of #4 — the multi-prior scorecard was missing the **guessed struct field offsets**
pattern named in the issue.

### What

* `probe_elf_shoff` (new): the model memorizes a textbook ELF64 layout in which a
  "typical small ELF" keeps its section header table at 0x1000, and asserts
  `e_shoff == 0x1000` (the u64 at file offset 0x28 of the ELF64 header) for any
  ELF64 binary. The prior is blind (never reads the section table) and the verdict
  goes through the verifier with the usual false-VERIFIED guard that re-reads the raw
  bytes. ELF64 only (`EI_CLASS == 2`): the ELF32 header lays `e_shoff` out
  differently, so the 64-bit memorized value is not a sound prior there.
* `tests/test_probes.py`: `TestElfShoffProbe` — refuted when the slot is not 0x1000,
  verified (not a false accept) when it is, inapplicable for ELF32 / PE, plus the
  guard-inversion case (a buggy VERIFIED whose raw bytes contradict the claim is
  flagged).
* `BENCHMARK.md`: probe table row + one aarch64 field run (33 ELFs under
  /usr/bin + /usr/lib on a Jetson): prior refuted on all 33, 0 false VERIFIED.
  Across the ~1,800 ELF64 binaries there, observed `e_shoff` ranges from 0x2a8 to
  0xbba8d38 and none equals 0x1000.

### Bonus fix in the same file

The `--probe` CLI filter never worked: the value-collection loop started *at* the
`--probe` token itself (which starts with `--`, so the loop body never ran), `only`
was always `None`, and the flag silently ran every probe. One-line fix (`i =
argv.index("--probe") + 1`). Verified: `--probe elf_shoff` now runs that probe only.

### Local verification

The README lists [Fireworks](https://fireworks.ai/) among the supported model providers, but a run configured for Fireworks fails before the first model call, and after fixing that it fails again on every query due to a response-validation bug in current opencode servers. fix: use async session API for heavy upload commands

Replaces blocking process.exec() calls in upload() with session-based execution (run_async=True + polling). The previous approach held a single HTTP connection open for minutes during cat/tar operations, which the Daytona server reset before the command completed.
